title: Role of government in microeconomics
summary: Governments intervene with price ceilings and floors, indirect taxes, subsidies, direct provision, regulation and nudges. Each has consequences for stakeholders. HL quantifies these effects.

keyterms.definition: A legal maximum price set below equilibrium to make a good affordable; it causes a shortage.
A legal minimum price set above equilibrium, e.g. to support farmers or workers; it causes a surplus.
A price floor in the labour market; if set above equilibrium it may cause unemployment.
Illegal trade at prices above a legal maximum, which often appears when a ceiling causes a shortage.
An indirect tax of a fixed amount per unit sold; supply shifts up parallel by the tax.
An indirect tax charged as a percentage of the price (e.g. VAT); the supply curve pivots upward.
How the burden of an indirect tax is shared between consumers and producers; consumers bear more when demand is inelastic.
The loss of social surplus when output differs from the allocatively efficient level.
When government itself supplies goods or services, e.g. state schools or hospitals.
Laws that limit or ban activities, e.g. age limits for alcohol or emission standards.
Any group affected by a policy, e.g. consumers, producers, workers, government and society.
Subsidy per unit × new quantity; an opportunity cost for government spending.
Tax per unit × quantity sold after the tax.

questions.prompt: A city sets a maximum rent below the equilibrium rent. What is the most likely result?
questions.explanation: At the lower price, Qd rises and Qs falls, creating excess demand.

questions.statement: A price floor is effective only if it is set above the equilibrium price.
questions.explanation: A floor below equilibrium has no effect because the market price is already higher.

questions.text: Illegal trade above a legal maximum price takes place on a ___ market.
questions.explanation: Shortages create incentives for buyers to pay more illegally.

questions.prompt: A government guarantees farmers a minimum price above equilibrium and buys the surplus. Who gains most directly?
questions.explanation: Farmers get higher prices and sell more; consumers pay more and taxpayers fund the purchases.

questions.prompt: Demand for cigarettes is price inelastic. Who bears most of a cigarette tax?
questions.explanation: When demand is inelastic, producers can pass most of the tax on as a higher price.

questions.prompt: Match each policy to its effect on the market.

pairs.right: Supply shifts up by a fixed amount

questions.explanation: Taxes raise firms’ costs; subsidies lower them; controls fix the price.

questions.statement: A minimum wage set above the market wage may cause unemployment.
questions.explanation: More workers want jobs and firms demand fewer, creating excess supply of labour.

questions.prompt: Which is a likely consequence of a subsidy to solar panel producers?
options: Lower price and higher output of solar panels
questions.explanation: Lower costs shift supply right; consumers pay less and buy more.

questions.text: A tax charged as a percentage of price, such as VAT, is an ___ tax.
questions.explanation: Ad valorem taxes rise with price, so the supply curve diverges from the original.

questions.prompt: Order the effects of a price ceiling on bread.
items: Quantity supplied falls and quantity demanded rises
Parallel markets or non-price rationing develop
questions.explanation: Shortages lead to queues, rationing and black markets.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of direct provision?
questions.explanation: Direct provision means government supplies the good itself.

questions.statement: Command and control regulation works by changing prices.
questions.explanation: Regulation uses rules and penalties rather than price signals.

questions.text: A group affected by a policy is called a ___.
questions.explanation: Evaluation of intervention considers effects on each stakeholder.

questions.prompt: Why do governments set price ceilings on staple foods?
options: To make necessities affordable for low-income households
questions.explanation: Equity is the main aim, but shortages can result.

questions.prompt: Which is a weakness of a price floor for farm products?
options: Taxpayers fund the purchase and storage of surpluses
questions.explanation: Surpluses must be bought, stored or destroyed: an opportunity cost for government.

questions.prompt: Match the intervention to a likely aim.

pairs.right: Increase consumption of a merit good

questions.explanation: Governments intervene to raise revenue, support groups or correct market failure.

questions.statement: All indirect taxes create a welfare loss in a competitive market without externalities.
questions.explanation: Output falls below the efficient level, losing some consumer and producer surplus.

questions.prompt: Which statement about tax incidence is correct?
options: Consumers always pay the full tax
The more price elastic the demand, the larger the share of the tax paid by producers
Producers always pay the full tax
Incidence does not depend on elasticity
questions.explanation: If consumers can easily switch away, firms cannot pass the tax on.

questions.text: The loss of social surplus caused by a policy that moves output away from the efficient level is a ___ loss.
questions.explanation: Also called deadweight loss.

questions.prompt: Order a structured evaluation of a sugar tax.
items: Explain how the tax shifts supply
Identify effects on consumers, producers and government
questions.explanation: Good evaluation considers stakeholders, time, and alternatives before concluding.

lessons.title: HL: Calculating the effects of intervention

questions.prompt: Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = −20 + 4P. A $3 per-unit tax is imposed, so Qs = −32 + 4P. What is the new price paid by consumers?
After the $3 tax, quantity is 56 units. What is government tax revenue?

questions.text: Before the tax P = $20; after it consumers pay $22 and firms keep $19. Per unit, consumers bear $___ of the tax.
questions.explanation: Consumers pay $2 more; producers receive $1 less. Demand is less elastic than supply here.

questions.statement: In this example, the total tax paid by producers is $56.
questions.explanation: Producer share = $1 × 56 units = $56; consumer share = $2 × 56 = $112.

questions.prompt: Same market (Qd = 100 − 2P, Qs = −20 + 4P). A maximum price of $15 is set. What is the shortage?
questions.explanation: Qd = 70 and Qs = 40 at $15, so excess demand = 30.

questions.prompt: A minimum price of $25 is set and the government buys the surplus. How much does it spend?
A $1.50 per-unit subsidy gives Qs = −14 + 4P. New equilibrium is P = $19, Q = 62. What is the cost of the subsidy?
questions.explanation: Cost = subsidy × quantity = 1.50 × 62 = $93.

questions.text: With the subsidy, producers receive $19 + $1.50 = $___ per unit.
questions.explanation: Producers get the market price plus the subsidy.

questions.prompt: Match each calculation to its formula.

pairs.right: Qd − Qs at the ceiling price

questions.explanation: These areas can be read from diagrams or calculated from functions.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to find the effect of a $t tax using functions.
items: Rewrite supply as Qs = c + d(P − t)
Set Qd equal to the new Qs and solve for P
Substitute to find the new quantity
Calculate revenue and each group’s share of the tax
questions.explanation: The tax lowers the price sellers keep by t at every consumer price.
